blocks.content: Mouse input moves the paddle by following the cursor. Keyboard input works differently.
Instead of reading a position, you track which keys are currently being held down.
You do this with boolean flags. A flag is just a variable that is either true or false. When a key is pressed it becomes true. When it is released it goes back to false.

Click Run Code, click on the canvas to give it focus, then use the arrow keys to move the paddle left and right.
Here, keydown sets the flag to true and keyup clears it to false. The update() function reads those flags every frame and moves the paddle if either arrow key is held.

The key insight is that the event handlers only update state - they never move the paddle directly. All movement happens inside update(), which runs exactly once per frame at a consistent 60fps. If you moved the paddle inside keydown, the OS key-repeat delay and repeat rate would make movement feel jerky and inconsistent across devices. Reading flags in the game loop gives smooth, frame-rate-locked movement every time.
We use keys[e.key] in the event handler because e.key is a string variable. In update() we use keys.ArrowLeft directly because we know the exact key name.
